Supermicro Appoints Mark Long As Senior Vice President And Chief Financial Officer
Super Micro Computer has appointed Mark Long as Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, effective immediately. He will report directly to Founder, President, and CEO Charles Liang.
Long succeeds David Weigand, who will assist with the transition before shifting his focus toward helping optimize and accelerate Supermicro’s business.
Long brings decades of experience across corporate finance, strategy, mergers and acquisitions, capital allocation, and technology infrastructure. He most recently served as Chief Financial Officer and Chief Strategy Officer of Western Digital, where he oversaw financial management, investor relations, and corporate strategy.
Earlier in his career, Long co-founded technology-focused investment firm Prime Impact Capital and served as a partner. He also previously held the role of Senior Vice President of Strategy and Corporate Development at Hitachi Global Storage Technologies.
Long also spent part of his career in investment banking, where his work focused on the software, cloud infrastructure, and storage sectors. Supermicro said it conducted an extensive search process to identify a candidate with the financial and strategic experience needed for the position.
The appointment comes as Supermicro continues expanding its AI and high-performance computing infrastructure business. The company develops servers, AI systems, storage products, networking infrastructure, software, and other data center technologies and is seeking to capitalize on continued growth in AI and IT infrastructure spending.
Supermicro said Long will play a key role in strengthening the company’s financial foundation, operational execution, and capital strategy while supporting its expansion across AI, cloud, enterprise, storage, and 5G and edge infrastructure markets.
KEY QUOTES:
“We are pleased to welcome Mark to the Supermicro executive team and look forward to benefitting from his deep strategic expertise and proven leadership. I’m confident Mark will have an immediate positive impact in strengthening and accelerating our operational and financial execution as we continue to scale our business to capture the next wave of AI and IT infrastructure growth.”
Charles Liang, Founder, President, And CEO Of Supermicro
“We are also grateful to David Weigand for his many years of service as CFO and for his support of an orderly transition.”
Charles Liang, Founder, President, And CEO Of Supermicro
“I am honored to join Supermicro as it continues to build on its leadership in AI and high-performance infrastructure. Charles has built a remarkable company, and I look forward to partnering closely with him and the executive team to scale the business effectively and efficiently – strengthening our financial foundation while supporting continued innovation, growth, and long-term value creation for shareholders.”
Mark Long, Senior Vice President And Chief Financial Officer Of Supermicro

Prediction: The Next Chapter of Supermicro Could Be More Important Than the Last
Supermicro booked $60 billion in new orders and targets $72 billion in revenue, yet Wall Street still rates it a near-sell. Here is what analysts are missing and the three conditions that could send shares to $70 by 2027.
Published October 6, 2026, 12:00pm ET · 3 min read
Price Targets desk. Editor: Vandita Jadeja.
Investing in stocks is a great way to build wealth and gain financial freedom. © Phongphan/Shutterstock.com
Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI | SMCI Price Prediction | SMCI Price Prediction) wants to be more than a server assembler. The San Jose company booked more than $60 billion in new orders last quarter. It now targets fiscal 2027 revenue of $65 billion to $72 billion, up from $39.1 billion in fiscal 2026.
Shares are up 48.31% year to date and still trade at about 10x forward earnings. That gap raises the question of whether Supermicro can hit $70 per share in 2027.
What’s Holding Supermicro Back Below Its 52-Week High
The stock has momentum: shares rose 4.58% over the past week and 18.25% over the past month. Even so, they are still down 17.14% over the past year.
Credibility weighs on the stock, as revenue missed estimates in five of the last six quarters. Fiscal 2026 operating cash flow came in at negative $6.8 billion, and the company raised $5.6 billion in equity.
Q1 gross margin guidance of 10.4% to 10.8% sits far below Q4’s 17.6%. An update on the board inquiry is still pending. The stock’s beta is 1.996, so each of these worries hits shares roughly twice as hard as the broader market.
Wall Street Sees No Upside. Our Model Says 12.4%
The consensus target is $42.38, about 2.4% below today’s $43.41. Analysts rate it 2 Strong Buys, 3 Buys, 11 Holds, 2 Sells and 1 Strong Sell. Our base case is $48.78, or 12.4% upside. The model’s range runs from $37.60 in the bear case to $53.54 in the bull case, and confidence is high at 0.9.
In my view, analysts are stuck on to old disappointments. Only 26% of them are bullish. In our adjustment, earnings growth contributed 0.03, five times the 0.006 from analyst views. Fundamentals are improving faster than the ratings.
Here’s What It Takes for Supermicro to Reach $70
Getting to $70 from the current $43.41 calls for a 61.3% gain. Forward EPS is $4.3382, so $70 equals to a forward P/E of 16x. Our base case already implies 12x, which means the bold target needs 5x of additional multiple expansion.
That seems achievable. Forward EPS already exceeds fiscal 2026’s $3.63, so the forward multiple falls if guidance holds. Enterprise and channel revenue rose 172% to $5.6 billion in Q4.
CEO Charles Liang said “we are improving profitability through a richer enterprise customer mix and broader adoption of our optimized Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS) architecture.”
Supermicro is one of the picks-and-shovels names behind the AI data-center expansion (we covered seven of these suppliers, from power to cooling, in a report you can download here). The main risk is that power and cooling delays push backlog shipments into later quarters.
Mizuho analyst Vijay Rakesh raised the firm’s price target on Super Micro to $43 from $35 and keeps a Neutral rating on the shares.
Supermicro Trades at a Discount to Its Earnings Power
At $43.41, shares trade at 10x forward EPS. That looks cheap for a business that grew revenue 78%, though cash flow concerns explain part of the discount.
Shares range from a 52-week low of $19.48 to a high of $58.78. Over 10 years, the stock has returned 1,748.02%. A $70 price would still leave Supermicro at a mid-teens multiple.
$70 Is a Stretch, but Here’s Why It’s Possible
Reaching $70 in 2027 calls for a 61.3% advance. I see it as a stretch that is still within reach. Three conditions must be met. First, record backlog has to convert into revenue near the top of guidance.
Second, gross margins need to hold as the enterprise and DCBBS mix grows. Third, operating cash flow has to turn positive without more dilution. Another revenue miss or a bad board inquiry outcome would ruin it. Investors shouldn’t expect this level of return every year, but we’ve outlined the plan for how Super Micro Computer could reach $70 in 2027.

Supermicro Appoints Shesha Krishnapura To Board Of Directors
Supermicro appointed Shesha Krishnapura as an independent member of its Board of Directors. Krishnapura brings 35 years of operational and technology experience from Intel.
His background includes high-performance computing, artificial intelligence infrastructure, hyperscale data centers, semiconductor design, and energy-efficient computing.
Krishnapura most recently served as an Intel Fellow and Chief Technology Officer of Intel IT.
In that position, he helped set technology strategy, architecture, and engineering governance for computing environments supporting Intel’s semiconductor design and development operations.
During his Intel career, Krishnapura led the development of 25 disaggregated server designs.
He also helped transform Intel’s D2 FAB into a LEED Platinum-certified hyperscale data center with more than 112 megawatts of capacity and a power usage effectiveness rating of 1.06.
Krishnapura has co-developed and co-taught a graduate-level high-performance computing course at Stanford University since 2016.
He holds six granted patents and has authored nearly 100 publications and technical whitepapers.
The appointment comes as Judy Lin retires from Supermicro’s Board after serving since 2022.
Supermicro said Krishnapura’s infrastructure and computing experience will support the company as it expands its Data Center Building Block Solutions business.

Super Micro (SMCI) Won Over $60 Billion in Orders, Is the Discount Deserved?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 9:15 PM CDT 4 min read
Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) has spent October fielding questions about a smuggling case. A contractor linked to the company pleaded guilty earlier this month to helping ship servers loaded with advanced Nvidia chips to China, Reuters reported. Prosecutors say the scheme involved billions of dollars of U.S. AI technology. The company says it wasn't named as a defendant and that the case hasn't affected its business operations. If you're looking for more undervalued stocks to play AI, check out our report on the 10 Undervalued AI Stocks to Buy Now.
But the business keeps getting bigger, and the stock is priced as if it won't. Its multiple of expected earnings sits far below the sector's. The question is whether that discount fairly reflects the legal risk, or whether it undervalues a company whose sales keep climbing. On the facts so far, the second reading looks closer, with one big condition attached.
The company builds the server racks that run AI data centers, including liquid-cooled systems for Nvidia's newest chips. Its customers range from cloud providers to ordinary businesses. Its pitch is pre-assembled building blocks that get a data center running faster than buying parts one by one.
Vertiv vs. Eaton: Which AI Power Stock Offers More Cash Flow for the Price?
Sales for the fiscal year that ended in June reached $39.1 billion, up from $22.0 billion a year earlier. CEO Charles Liang said the company took in more than $60 billion of new orders over the year and added several hundred enterprise customers. It also entered the new year with a record backlog. Management is guiding to $65.0 billion to $72.0 billion in sales for fiscal 2027, a range whose low end sits well above all of last year. If you're interested in AI infrastructure, we recently compiled a report on 10 Fastest-Growing AI Infrastructure Stocks to Buy.
This kind of growth has a long record behind it. Over the past five years, sales have grown about 61.5% a year, so the latest jump extends a long run instead of starting one.
Growth has come with thin margins, and that is where the surprise sits. Gross margin for the full year was 10.8%. Then, in the June quarter, it jumped to 17.5%, and net income for the quarter reached $1,178 million, well above the year-earlier quarter.
A single quarter can't prove a new level. Over the past 12 months, operating margin was only 7.09%, so most of the year still looked like a low-margin business. If the June quarter holds, though, the company will earn far more on each dollar of sales than the full-year figure suggests.
The discount comes down to trust, and the Reuters report gives investors reasons to ask for it. Co-founder Yih-Shyan Liaw, who joined the board in 2023, and a former sales manager in Taiwan were also indicted in the same case. The indictment says the servers carried Nvidia chips that U.S. rules restrict, and it describes the scheme as starting around October 2023.
Management says it fired the contractor and cut ties with the other defendants earlier this year. Last week it also named a new chief financial officer, Mark Long, who reports directly to Liang. Neither step answers whether controls were tight when the shipments left. Because its newest racks are built around Nvidia chips, a wider probe or new limits on shipments would hit the product investors are paying for. Investors who want more on stocks falling out of favor can see our ranking of 10 Stocks Investors Are Running Away From.
At 7.29 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, based on adjusted figures, the stock sits well below the sector median of 21.01 and below its own five-year average of 16.36. The consensus forecast calls for earnings per share to grow 19.49% for that year, so the market isn't pricing in a shrinking company. For investors looking for cheaper growth, our list of 10 Undervalued Growth Stocks to Buy Now is worth a look.
If you own the shares, you're effectively betting that the legal problems stay with a few individuals and don't reach the numbers. The multiple leaves room for the sales guidance to fall short and still look cheap.
The discount looks too deep for a company with this much demand behind it, unless the export case widens. What decides it is the next report: whether gross margin stays near the June quarter's 17.5% or slides back toward the 10.8% of the full year.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of SMCI as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. Digi Power X pairs owned power infrastructure with Supermicro GPUs to serve enterprise AI customers Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock
Digi Power X Inc (NASDAQ:DGXX, FRA:1NQ0, NEO:DGX) is using Super Micro Computer Inc (NASDAQ:SMCI) servers built around Nvidia's latest Blackwell chips to sell AI computing capacity to enterprise customers, according to a Supermicro case study.
The company owns and operates the infrastructure behind its NeoCloudz platform, from power generation and substations to Tier III data centers. NeoCloudz rents GPU capacity on dedicated bare-metal servers, with no virtualization layer and no sharing of hardware among customers. The servers can be hosted at a Digi Power X facility or installed at a customer's site.
Digi Power X deployed Supermicro systems with Nvidia B200 and B300 GPUs, liquid cooling and Supermicro management software, the case study highlighted.
Supermicro said it wanted hardware that could handle both large-scale AI training and real-time inference.
The company said its ownership of power assets, including substations and on-site generation, sets it apart from traditional cloud providers. It said GPU rental rates reflect its actual power costs rather than the margins charged by those providers. It also said liquid-cooled, high-density racks fit more computing into less floor space, which lowers the cost per GPU-hour passed on to customers. As a result, Digi Power X said, it can offer Blackwell compute at rates traditional providers can't match.
Scalability was another priority. Digi Power X said it aims to add capacity in weeks rather than years, without large upfront capital outlays at each stage of growth.
For orchestration and billing, the company integrated three Supermicro software products: SuperCloud Composer, SuperCloud Developer Experience and SuperCloud Director. They give customers visibility into their workloads and automated, metered billing.
The data center environment includes high-density GPU rack rows with per-cabinet power monitoring, hot-aisle containment, expansion-ready room layouts and rack-level environmental sensing.
"DigiPowerX was built on the conviction that the AI infrastructure market needed a fundamentally different model — one where the operator controls the full stack, from power to compute, and passes those structural advantages directly to customers," said Alec Amar, president of Digi Power X.
"Supermicro has been a critical partner in executing that vision, giving us access to the latest NVIDIA Blackwell hardware and the software tooling to manage it at scale. The result is a platform we are proud to be already running in production for enterprise AI customers today."
The platform is already running in production for enterprise customers, the case study said.

Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI | SMCI Price Prediction | SMCI Price Prediction) wants to be more than a server assembler. The San Jose company booked more than $60 billion in new orders last quarter. It now targets fiscal 2027 revenue of $65 billion to $72 billion, up from $39.1 billion in fiscal 2026.
Shares are up 48.31% year to date and still trade at about 10x forward earnings. That gap raises the question of whether Supermicro can hit $70 per share in 2027.
What’s Holding Supermicro Back Below Its 52-Week High
The stock has momentum: shares rose 4.58% over the past week and 18.25% over the past month. Even so, they are still down 17.14% over the past year.
Credibility weighs on the stock, as revenue missed estimates in five of the last six quarters. Fiscal 2026 operating cash flow came in at negative $6.8 billion, and the company raised $5.6 billion in equity.
Q1 gross margin guidance of 10.4% to 10.8% sits far below Q4’s 17.6%. An update on the board inquiry is still pending. The stock’s beta is 1.996, so each of these worries hits shares roughly twice as hard as the broader market.
Wall Street Sees No Upside. Our Model Says 12.4%
The consensus target is $42.38, about 2.4% below today’s $43.41. Analysts rate it 2 Strong Buys, 3 Buys, 11 Holds, 2 Sells and 1 Strong Sell. Our base case is $48.78, or 12.4% upside. The model’s range runs from $37.60 in the bear case to $53.54 in the bull case, and confidence is high at 0.9.
In my view, analysts are stuck on to old disappointments. Only 26% of them are bullish. In our adjustment, earnings growth contributed 0.03, five times the 0.006 from analyst views. Fundamentals are improving faster than the ratings.
Here’s What It Takes for Supermicro to Reach $70
Getting to $70 from the current $43.41 calls for a 61.3% gain. Forward EPS is $4.3382, so $70 equals to a forward P/E of 16x. Our base case already implies 12x, which means the bold target needs 5x of additional multiple expansion.
That seems achievable. Forward EPS already exceeds fiscal 2026’s $3.63, so the forward multiple falls if guidance holds. Enterprise and channel revenue rose 172% to $5.6 billion in Q4.
CEO Charles Liang said “we are improving profitability through a richer enterprise customer mix and broader adoption of our optimized Data Center Building Block Solutions (DCBBS) architecture.”
Supermicro is one of the picks-and-shovels names behind the AI data-center expansion (we covered seven of these suppliers, from power to cooling, in a report you can download here). The main risk is that power and cooling delays push backlog shipments into later quarters.
Mizuho analyst Vijay Rakesh raised the firm’s price target on Super Micro to $43 from $35 and keeps a Neutral rating on the shares.
Supermicro Trades at a Discount to Its Earnings Power
At $43.41, shares trade at 10x forward EPS. That looks cheap for a business that grew revenue 78%, though cash flow concerns explain part of the discount.
Shares range from a 52-week low of $19.48 to a high of $58.78. Over 10 years, the stock has returned 1,748.02%. A $70 price would still leave Supermicro at a mid-teens multiple.
$70 Is a Stretch, but Here’s Why It’s Possible
Reaching $70 in 2027 calls for a 61.3% advance. I see it as a stretch that is still within reach. Three conditions must be met. First, record backlog has to convert into revenue near the top of guidance.
Second, gross margins need to hold as the enterprise and DCBBS mix grows. Third, operating cash flow has to turn positive without more dilution. Another revenue miss or a bad board inquiry outcome would ruin it. Investors shouldn’t expect this level of return every year, but we’ve outlined the plan for how Super Micro Computer could reach $70 in 2027.

Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) has spent October fielding questions about a smuggling case. A contractor linked to the company pleaded guilty earlier this month to helping ship servers loaded with advanced Nvidia chips to China, Reuters reported. Prosecutors say the scheme involved billions of dollars of U.S. AI technology. The company says it wasn't named as a defendant and that the case hasn't affected its business operations. But the business keeps getting bigger, and the stock is priced as if it won't. Its multiple of expected earnings sits far below the sector's. The question is whether that discount fairly reflects the legal risk, or whether it undervalues a company whose sales keep climbing. On the facts so far, the second reading looks closer, with one big condition attached.
The company builds the server racks that run AI data centers, including liquid-cooled systems for Nvidia's newest chips. Its customers range from cloud providers to ordinary businesses. Its pitch is pre-assembled building blocks that get a data center running faster than buying parts one by one.

Sales for the fiscal year that ended in June reached $39.1 billion, up from $22.0 billion a year earlier. CEO Charles Liang said the company took in more than $60 billion of new orders over the year and added several hundred enterprise customers. It also entered the new year with a record backlog. Management is guiding to $65.0 billion to $72.0 billion in sales for fiscal 2027, a range whose low end sits well above all of last year. This kind of growth has a long record behind it. Over the past five years, sales have grown about 61.5% a year, so the latest jump extends a long run instead of starting one.
Growth has come with thin margins, and that is where the surprise sits. Gross margin for the full year was 10.8%. Then, in the June quarter, it jumped to 17.5%, and net income for the quarter reached $1,178 million, well above the year-earlier quarter.
A single quarter can't prove a new level. Over the past 12 months, operating margin was only 7.09%, so most of the year still looked like a low-margin business. If the June quarter holds, though, the company will earn far more on each dollar of sales than the full-year figure suggests.
The discount comes down to trust, and the Reuters report gives investors reasons to ask for it. Co-founder Yih-Shyan Liaw, who joined the board in 2023, and a former sales manager in Taiwan were also indicted in the same case. The indictment says the servers carried Nvidia chips that U.S. rules restrict, and it describes the scheme as starting around October 2023.
Management says it fired the contractor and cut ties with the other defendants earlier this year. Last week it also named a new chief financial officer, Mark Long, who reports directly to Liang. Neither step answers whether controls were tight when the shipments left. Because its newest racks are built around Nvidia chips, a wider probe or new limits on shipments would hit the product investors are paying for. At 7.29 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, based on adjusted figures, the stock sits well below the sector median of 21.01 and below its own five-year average of 16.36. The consensus forecast calls for earnings per share to grow 19.49% for that year, so the market isn't pricing in a shrinking company. If you own the shares, you're effectively betting that the legal problems stay with a few individuals and don't reach the numbers. The multiple leaves room for the sales guidance to fall short and still look cheap.
The discount looks too deep for a company with this much demand behind it, unless the export case widens. What decides it is the next report: whether gross margin stays near the June quarter's 17.5% or slides back toward the 10.8% of the full year.
